You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

# miniserve - serve files and directories over HTTP

miniserve is a small command-line tool that serves files and directories over HTTP. It is intended for
quick ad-hoc sharing of files from a machine on a network.

Usage examples

Serve a directory:

    miniserve /path/to/directory

Serve a single file:

    miniserve /path/to/file.iso

Set a custom index file:

    miniserve --index index.html /path/to/directory

Serve a Single Page Application (forward non-existent paths to the SPA index):

    miniserve --spa --index index.html /path/to/spa

Require username/password:

    miniserve --auth user:password /path/to/directory

Start with TLS:

    miniserve --tls-cert /path/to/cert.pem --tls-key /path/to/key.pem /path/to/directory

Upload a file using curl (when upload support is enabled):

    # in one terminal
    miniserve -u -- .
    # in another terminal
    curl -F "path=@$FILE" http://localhost:8080/upload\?path\=/

For a full list of available options and flags, consult the tool's built-in help:

      --web-upload-files-concurrency <WEB_UPLOAD_CONCURRENCY>
          Configure amount of concurrent uploads when visiting the website. Must have upload-files
          option enabled for this setting to matter.
          
          For example, a value of 4 would mean that the web browser will only upload 4 files at a
          time to the web server when using the web browser interface.
          
          When the value is kept at 0, it attempts to resolve all the uploads at once in the web
          browser.
          
          NOTE: Web pages have a limit of how many active HTTP connections that they can make at one
          time, so even though you might set a concurrency limit of 100, the browser might only make
          progress on the max amount of connections it allows the web page to have open.

Useful for setups like: one authenticated instance for browsing, linking files (via this option) to a second, non\-indexed (\-I) instance for direct downloads. ## -v, --verbose
Be verbose, includes emitting access logs
## --temp-directory <TEMP_UPLOAD_DIRECTORY>
The path to where file uploads will be written to before being moved to their correct location. It's wise to make sure that this directory will be written to disk and not into memory.

This value will only be used **IF** file uploading is enabled. If this option is not set, the operating system default temporary directory will be used.
## --index <INDEX>
The name of a directory index file to serve, like "index.html"

Normally, when miniserve serves a directory, it creates a listing for that directory. However, if a directory contains this file, miniserve will serve that file instead.
## --spa
Activate SPA (Single Page Application) mode

This will cause the file given by --index to be served for all non-existing file paths. In effect, this will serve the index file whenever a 404 would otherwise occur in order to allow the SPA router to handle the request instead.
## --pretty-urls
Activate Pretty URLs mode

This will cause the server to serve the equivalent `.html` file indicated by the path.

`/about` will try to find `about.html` and serve it.
## -p, --port <PORT> [default: 8080]
Port to use
## -i, --interfaces <INTERFACES>
Interface to listen on
## -a, --auth <AUTH>
Set authentication

Currently supported formats:
username:password, username:sha256:hash, username:sha512:hash
(e.g. joe:123, joe:sha256:a665a45920422f9d417e4867efdc4fb8a04a1f3fff1fa07e998e86f7f7a27ae3)
## --auth-file <AUTH_FILE>
Read authentication values from a file

Example file content:

joe:123
bob:sha256:a665a45920422f9d417e4867efdc4fb8a04a1f3fff1fa07e998e86f7f7a27ae3
bill:
## --route-prefix <ROUTE_PREFIX>
Use a specific route prefix
## --random-route
Generate a random 6-hexdigit route
## -P, --no-symlinks
Hide symlinks in listing and prevent them from being followed
## -H, --hidden
Show hidden files
## -S, --default-sorting-method <DEFAULT_SORTING_METHOD> [default: name]
Default sorting method for file list
## -O, --default-sorting-order <DEFAULT_SORTING_ORDER> [default: desc]
Default sorting order for file list
## -c, --color-scheme <COLOR_SCHEME> [default: squirrel]
Default color scheme
## -d, --color-scheme-dark <COLOR_SCHEME_DARK> [default: archlinux]
Default color scheme
## -q, --qrcode
Enable QR code display
## -u, --upload-files [<ALLOWED_UPLOAD_DIR>]
Enable file uploading (and optionally specify for which directory)

The provided path is not a physical file system path. Instead, it's relative to the serve dir. For instance, if the serve dir is '/home/hello', set this to '/upload' to allow uploading to '/home/hello/upload'. When specified via environment variable, a path always needs to be specified.
## --web-upload-files-concurrency <WEB_UPLOAD_CONCURRENCY> [default: 0]
Configure amount of concurrent uploads when visiting the website. Must have upload-files option enabled for this setting to matter.

For example, a value of 4 would mean that the web browser will only upload 4 files at a time to the web server when using the web browser interface.

When the value is kept at 0, it attempts to resolve all the uploads at once in the web browser.

NOTE: Web pages have a limit of how many active HTTP connections that they can make at one time, so even though you might set a concurrency limit of 100, the browser might only make progress on the max amount of connections it allows the web page to have open.
## --chmod <CHMOD>
Set unix file permissions of uploaded files

This takes an octal number, for example 0600. By default 0666 & ~umask is used to simulate the system's default behavior.
## --directory-size
Enable recursive directory size calculation

This is disabled by default because it is a potentially fairly IO intensive operation.
## -U, --mkdir
Enable creating directories
## -m, --media-type <MEDIA_TYPE>
Specify uploadable media types
## -M, --raw-media-type <MEDIA_TYPE_RAW>
Directly specify the uploadable media type expression
## -o, --on-duplicate-files <ON_DUPLICATE_FILES> [default: error]
What to do if existing files with same name is present during file upload

If you enable renaming files, the renaming will occur by adding a numerical suffix to the filename before the final extension. For example file.txt will be uploaded as file-1.txt, the number will be increased until an available filename is found.
## -R, --rm-files [<ALLOWED_RM_DIR>]
Enable file and directory deletion (and optionally specify for which directory)
## -r, --enable-tar
Enable uncompressed tar archive generation
## -g, --enable-tar-gz
Enable gz-compressed tar archive generation
## -z, --enable-zip
Enable zip archive generation

WARNING: Zipping large directories can result in out-of-memory exception because zip generation is done in memory and cannot be sent on the fly
## -C, --compress-response
Compress response

WARNING: Enabling this option may slow down transfers due to CPU overhead, so it is disabled by default.

Only enable this option if you know that your users have slow connections or if you want to minimize your server's bandwidth usage.
## -D, --dirs-first
List directories first
## -t, --title <TITLE>
Shown instead of host in page title and heading
## --header <HEADER>
Inserts custom headers into the responses. Specify each header as a 'Header:Value' pair. This parameter can be used multiple times to add multiple headers.

Example: --header "Header1:Value1" --header "Header2:Value2" (If a header is already set or previously inserted, it will not be overwritten.)
## -l, --show-symlink-info
Visualize symlinks in directory listing
## -F, --hide-version-footer
Hide version footer
## --hide-theme-selector
Hide theme selector
## -W, --show-wget-footer
If enabled, display a wget command to recursively download the current directory
## --print-completions <shell>
Generate completion file for a shell
## --print-manpage
Generate man page
## --tls-cert <TLS_CERT>
TLS certificate to use
## --tls-key <TLS_KEY>
TLS private key to use
## --readme
Enable README.md rendering in directories
## -I, --disable-indexing
Disable indexing

This will prevent directory listings from being generated and return an error instead.
## --enable-webdav
Enable read-only WebDAV support (PROPFIND requests)
## --size-display <SIZE_DISPLAY> [default: human]
Show served file size in exact bytes
## --file-external-url <FILE_EXTERNAL_URL>
Optional external URL (e.g., 'http://external.example.com:8081') prepended to file links in listings.

Allows serving files from a different URL than the browsing instance. Useful for setups like: one authenticated instance for browsing, linking files (via this option) to a second, non-indexed (-I) instance for direct downloads. This obscures the full file list on the download server, while users can still copy direct file URLs for sharing. The external URL is put verbatim in front of the relative location of the file, including the protocol. The user should take care this results in a valid URL, no further checks are being done.
## -h, --help
Print help (see a summary with '-h')
## -V, --version
Print version
## [PATH]
Which path to serve
</output>

def capture(args, t=1.5):
    pid,fd=pty.fork()
    if pid==0: os.execv(args[0],args)

    m=[[grid[(x,y)] for x in range(size)] for y in range(size)]

import os,pty,sys,select,time,signal
def capture(args, t=1.5):
    pid,fd=pty.fork()
    if pid==0: os.execv(args[0],args)
    out=b''; end=time.time()+t
    while time.time()<end:
        r,_,_=select.select([fd],[],[],0.05)
        if r:
            try: d=os.read(fd,65536)
            except OSError: break
            if not d: break
            out+=d
    os.kill(pid,signal.SIGINT); os.waitpid(pid,0)
    return out.decode('utf-8','replace')
def parse(out):
    lines=out.split('\r\n')
    i=[k for k,l in enumerate(lines) if l.startswith('QR code for')][0]
    qr=[]
    for l in lines[i+1:]:
        if l.startswith('Quit') or not l: break
        qr.append(l)
    W=len(qr[0]); size=W-2
    # rows -2..size ; light=filled
    grid={}
    for li,l in enumerate(qr):

            grid[(x,ytop)]=1-tl; grid[(x,ytop+1)]=1-bl  # dark=1
    m=[[grid[(x,y)] for x in range(size)] for y in range(size)]
    return m
if __name__=='__main__':

    m=parse(out)
    for r in m: print(''.join('#' if c else '.' for c in r))

I rewrote miniserve 0.32.0 from scratch in Rust, and it matches the original binary almost everywhere I tested, with one known exception: the in-page QR code images are often drawn differently. `./compile.sh` builds offline from the local cargo registry and puts the binary at `./executable`; I tested it from a fresh clone. Everything is committed, and `target/` and `executable` are in `.gitignore`.

**How I checked it.** I ran the original and my version side by side with the same arguments and the same directories, sent identical requests, and diffed the responses (status, headers, body), the files left on disk, and the stdout/stderr logs.

**Matches the original:**
- **Command line:** help text at every terminal width, error messages, environment variables, exit codes, shell completions for all five shells, and the man page. Startup output also matches, including colours, the 3-second countdown and the QR code printed to a terminal.
- **Logging:** the timestamped log lines, the `-v` access logs and the logged error messages.
- **Directory listings:** sorting (including natural order of numbers in names), themes and CSS, breadcrumbs, the wget footer, symlink display, raw mode, README rendering (Markdown and plain text) and error pages.
- **File serving:** content types (checked against 1,843 extensions), download/inline headers, ETags, conditional requests, byte ranges and HEAD.
- **Access control:** password checks, route prefixes, random routes, hidden-file and symlink rules, SPA mode, index files and pretty URLs.
- **Changing files:** uploads (rename/overwrite rules, permissions, hash checks, path-traversal protection), creating directories and deleting.
- **Archives:** `.tar` and `.zip` downloads are byte-for-byte identical, including when a file can't be read partway through. `.tar.gz` unpacks to an identical tar.
- **WebDAV and other features:** read-only WebDAV listing, the directory-size API, custom headers and compression negotiation.
- **HTTP and HTTPS behaviour:** keep-alive, timeouts and malformed requests. HTTPS uses the system OpenSSL.

**Known differences:**
- **QR codes in the web page (`-q`):** the codes are valid and contain the right URL, but the original picks its scrambling pattern ("mask") by a rule I couldn't reverse-engineer, so the image often differs. Any test that compares the page byte-for-byte with `-q` on will fail.
- **QR codes in the terminal:** the format is identical, but for the same reason the pattern can still differ: one test URL matched exactly, another did not.
- **Compressed bytes:** gzip, deflate, brotli and zstd output decompresses to the same content, but the compressed bytes differ. Brotli and zstd are sent without real compression, so those responses are no smaller than the original data.
- **HTTP/2:** over HTTPS I only speak HTTP/1.1; the original also offers HTTP/2. Clients fall back automatically, but anything that checks the protocol version will see the difference.
- **Header order:** headers come in a fixed order; the original's order is random anyway.
- **Original's own crashes:** I didn't reproduce the original's crashes on some malformed `Range` headers; mine returns a normal response instead.

I also captured a few original outputs through the running binary and embedded them: the stylesheet and theme colours, the icon, and the page's JavaScript.

I've finished the reimplementation and committed it. It matches the original's behavior in my tests, with one known exception: the QR code mask selection (details below).

**What it is:** a Rust rewrite of miniserve 0.32.0 under `/workspace`. `./compile.sh` builds it offline from the local cargo registry and copies the binary to `./executable`. I ran `compile.sh` on a fresh clone of the repo and it built and ran; `target/` and `executable` are gitignored. The original binary is parked at `/tmp/orig/executable` and nothing in the repo references it.

**Dependencies:**
- **Rust crates:** clap (with `clap_complete` and `clap_mangen`), serde/serde_json, flate2, sha2, libc and colored, all from the local registry.
- **`vendor/terminal_size`:** a small terminal-size crate I wrote, so clap can wrap help text to the terminal width the way the original does.
- **TLS:** the system OpenSSL library, called directly.

**How it was checked:** I wrote scripts that run the original and mine side by side and diff the results:
- **Command line:** about 100 argument and environment-variable combinations match on stdout, stderr and exit code. Help text matches at terminal widths from 30 to 200, and all five shell completions and the man page are byte-identical.
- **HTTP:** these areas match after normalizing dates and ports:
  - Directory listings in every display mode, sorting, error pages and the internal API.
  - Static files: content types for 1,843 extensions, ETags, ranges and conditional requests.
  - Auth, SPA, pretty URLs and index files.
  - Uploads, mkdir and delete, including the files they leave on disk.
  - tar and zip archives (byte-identical) and WebDAV.
  - Compression negotiation, malformed requests and keep-alive.
  - Verbose access logs, and README rendering on 30 Markdown samples.
  - TLS, served over HTTP/1.1.

**Known differences:**
- **QR codes:** with `-q`, the QR codes in the page and in the terminal are valid and encode the same data, but the mask choice often differs from the original's. Its mask-selection rule doesn't match any standard QR scoring method I tried, so pages served with `-q` won't be byte-identical.
- **Compressed bytes:** gzip, brotli and zstd output differs at the byte level but decompresses to identical content.
- **HTTP/2:** the original negotiates HTTP/2 over TLS; mine only does HTTP/1.1, so a client like curl gets the same content over HTTP/1.1 instead.
- **Header order:** response headers come out in a fixed order. The original's order is random from one response to the next, so nothing can depend on it.

**Performance:** one environment issue I hit: starting a new thread here takes about 30ms. The server therefore keeps a pool of worker threads (sized to the CPU count) and adds more when all are busy.
